https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Consumer sentiment dropped to record lows earlier this summer as Americans said they were struggling to afford gas and groceries. Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Consumer sentiment dropped to record lows earlier this summer as Americans said they were struggling to afford gas and groceries. Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images Inflation US consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costs Annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4% Gaya Gupta Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.38 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US consumer prices remained stubbornly high in August as the end of the ceasefire between the US and Iran pushed energy prices up, according to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Friday. The annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, the same as it was in July. The most recent peak was seen in May, when the inflation rate hit a three-year high at 4.2%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, increased 0.3% from the month before and 2.4% annually. Gasoline increased 27.4% compared with the year before, accounting for more than one-third of the overall monthly increase in prices. Fuel , which is used to power and heat homes, increased annually at a staggering 52%. Prices of common grocery store essentials, such as meat, poultry, eggs and dairy, increased slightly, from 0.1% to 0.3%. Lettuce prices continued to fall, probably continued fallout from the cyclosporiasis outbreak . Despite dipping from its most recent peak, inflation remained above levels that were seen before the war in Iran , largely because of higher energy prices. On Friday, the cost of diesel, used for trucks, buses and trains, rose past $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, also surpassed $108 on Friday, its highest level since May. Meanwhile, gas prices at the pump sat at an average of $4.29 a gallon, $1.10 higher than the average a year ago, according to AAA . A line chart showing latest US inflation figures It’s a worrying sign for Republicans, who are on the ballot at a time when consumer sentiment has hit record lows and Americans say they are struggling to afford gas and groceries. Concerns over inflation have also bled into the US bond market, where the yields on some US treasurys have reached their highest points since the 2008 recession. Yet it’s unclear when relief will come. Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation Read more The White House is aware of what this could mean for the upcoming elections. On Wednesday night, Trump said Americans would get a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans win a majority in the midterms, which critics said was akin to bribery. One of the most direct ways the federal government can affect prices comes from the power of the US Federal Reserve , which sets the interest rates that have an effect on the price of loans, including mortgages, car payments and student debt. With prices remaining stubbornly high and core inflation rising, Friday’s report bolsters the likelihood that the Fed will vote to increase rates at its board meeting next week.. Either move could have heavy implications for the US economy . In a social media post last week, Trump said the central bank “must get smart” and lower rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he declared. But pressure to increase rates has been growing. At the Fed’s last board meeting in July, it voted 9-3 to maintain rates – the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Historically, raising interest rates helps to lower inflation – making investments more expensive slows the economy. Inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high, in 2022. After the Fed spent the next few years increasing interest rates, up to a range of 5.25%-5.5%, inflation went down to 2.3% in April 2025. Interest rates now sit at a range of 3.5%-3.75%, two percentage points lower than where they were two years ago. With inflation back up, some Fed economists have said it might be time for higher interest rates. Last week, the Fed governor Christopher Waller said there was “considerable uncertainty about how military conflicts, trade policy, and artificial intelligence will affect prices and economic activity” and it might be appropriate to raise rates if inflation showed no signs of easing. “If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level,” he said at a Reuters event. “But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.” The Fed’s new chair, Kevin Warsh, has made it clear the central bank will combat inflation during his tenure and achieve price stability. During a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last month, Warsh said that underlying inflation trends had not “meaningfully improved” over the summer. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” Warsh said. https://www.politico.eu/article/security.text: DUBLIN — A bare-knuckled attack on one of Ireland’s best-known politicians has the country questioning how much longer its leaders can go about their business without security. A Dublin man was arrested Thursday for allegedly assaulting Michael Healy-Rae as the independent lawmaker drove out of the capital back toward his distant County Kerry constituency . Police said they had recovered video footage showing a man approach Healy-Rae, 59, as he was sitting in rush-hour traffic Wednesday behind the wheel of his Skoda, which was emblazoned with the politician’s name and constituency contact details. Advertisement Advertisement Healy-Rae had his window rolled down and was talking on the phone to his son Jackie, a Kerry councilman, as a man walked into the road and started punching the politician in the face. While the attacker fled on foot, police helped Healy-Rae reach a nearby hospital to have his facial wounds stitched up. Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the attack on Healy-Rae — who had been a junior minister in his coalition government before his surprise resignation in April — could mark a watershed in how Irish politicians operate in public. “We’ve never had this before in our society,” said Martin, who has represented the southwest city of Cork in parliament since 1989. Reflecting the relative informality and openness of Irish political life, the prime minister spent part of this own week pressing the flesh with thousands of farmers at the National Ploughing Championships , one of the country’s perennial events featuring face-to-face contact with politicians from all parties. But there, too, Martin, faced an attempted assault and a suddenly beefed-up security detail. “Our democracy is relatively unusual in the sense that our members of parliament, and indeed ministers and myself, can walk through our streets unhindered,” said Martin, who called the attack on Healy-Rae “a significant moment that we have to take very seriously.” Healy-Rae, who was recovering Thursday at his Kerry home, issued a statement vowing he would “not be deterred” from politics. Advertisement Advertisement The flat-capped Kerryman , whose family has built a legendary political machine based on door-to-door house calls, appealed for “a serious conversation about the growing toxicity directed towards politicians and public representatives.” His son, who heard the assault unfold live on their phone call, said many months of social media attacks, particularly by anti-immigrant extremists, were fueling vitriol against his father — examples of which can be readily seen in comments on many of Healy-Rae’s recent social media posts. “Unfortunately it’s becoming more normal,” said Jackie Healy-Rae, who added: “I do honestly believe that it is only a matter of time before an Irish politician will be seriously injured or killed in this country.” Bloodshed once was a feature of Irish political life. Dozens of politicians died during Ireland’s 1919-21 war of independence from Britain and the resultant civil war of 1922-23, most famously IRA chieftain-turned-dealmaker Michael Collins . Three more politicians in the Republic of Ireland were slain as part of the three-decade conflict over the neighboring U.K. territory of Northern Ireland. But that threat ended with the region’s mid-1990s paramilitary cease-fires capped by a 1998 peace accord. Ireland’s government has been struggling since 2023 with a rise in street-level hostility against politicians, publishing findings that found particular hostility directed online against female lawmakers. It introduced reimbursements of up to €25,000 for beefing up security at politicians’ homes and constituency offices, where many of the country’s 174 members of the Dáil Éireann parliament meet weekly with the public to field their complaints.

Photograph: Lauren Powell Helen Haines ‘I don’t want to be known as a hero’: barber who rushed to help Helen Haines praised by PM Ricky Jefferies says he had just finished cutting hair when he grabbed and held the driver who allegedly deliberately struck the Indi MP Follow our Helen Haines live blog for latest updates Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Cait Kelly in Wangaratta Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.49 EDT First published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Australian prime minister has hailed him a hero for rushing out of his shop to help independent MP Helen Haines after she was allegedly run down in a deliberate attack – but barber Ricky Jefferies says he had “no choice” but to intervene. Standing on Tuesday morning outside his shop, which is right next to Haines’ electorate office in Wangaratta, Jefferies was almost shy about the whole thing. “I don’t want to be known as a hero,” the regional Victorian barber repeatedly told the large media pack that surrounded him. Car allegedly did U-turn and struck Helen Haines twice, as ‘hero’ local barber praised for apprehending driver Read more Jefferies spoke about how he had just finished cutting a young family’s hair when a car hit Haines at about 4pm on Monday. When he heard the loud crash, he ran to help. “A lot of people a lot of people got involved immediately, and they didn’t even check the danger,” he said. “They just ran to help. The driver was still in the car, the car was still on, and … one man sat in front of the moving car,” he said. “I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Haines was allegedly rammed twice on Murphy Street in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon, and remains in a critical but stable condition on Tuesday morning. The prime minister alleged it was an attack and it “wasn’t an accident”. Haines’ alleged attacker, who was arrested at the scene, has been named as 43-year-old Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent , Guardian Australia has confirmed. Witnesses have described the driver as doing a U-turn before allegedly ramming Haines against a vehicle, then reversing before doing it a second time, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said on Tuesday morning. Jefferies said after getting the driver out of the car, he held the man down. He said he told him he couldn’t leave but that the man would be alright, in an attempt to calm him while others helped Haines. He also alleged the man had a knife on him. “He did have a knife. He didn’t pull it out. Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away,” he alleged. Jefferies, who was back at work cutting hair at 7am on Tuesday, said he didn’t stop to think about the danger, only that his wife might be upset if he got hurt. “[I just thought] my wife will be disappointed if I’m injured,” he said. “My family is everything, and my community is second to that. “I was just trying to not get injured and not let anyone else be injured after the initial incident.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Jefferies actions have been widely commended on Tuesday, including by Albanese, Burke and the mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant. What happens to accidental heroes when the headlines fade? ‘You get your award and then there’s nothing’ Read more “It’s got to be said here that at this dark and terrible time, an element of light is the fact that a good Samaritan, someone rushed to Helen’s defence in Wangaratta … and that person is a hero today,” Albanese told the Today Show. “And I just think that he deserves enormous praise and thanks for his intervention, which could have prevented even further infliction of damage, which was aimed at Helen.” Grant said she had spoken to the barber on Tuesday morning, saying he was taking it in his stride. “He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.” Jefferies brushed the accolades aside, saying he doesn’t want to be seen as a hero and that – like all of the community – he is praying Haines recovers quickly. “No one’s job should put them at risk. I can tell you from my own personal dealings that she is a genuine, kind person,” he said. “I don’t think I’m the hero, I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way.” Explore more on these topics Helen Haines Victoria Australian politics Anthony Albanese news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Live Helen Haines live updates: MP critical but stable as AFP look into charges carrying up to 10 years’ imprisonment Car allegedly did U-turn and struck Helen Haines twice, in what some believe was targeted attack against MP Helen Haines is in a critical condition after an alleged attack. Read these reports instead 5 A place of error or mistakenness: Finding Nobel Laureate Anne Carson in translation 6 UP poll panel orders deactivation of computer operators’ ECINET login IDs after misuse allegations 7 Haryana: 8-year-old boy bangs KG student’s head against desk, hits her with brick inside classroom 8 Air pollution: 50% office staff to work from home in Gurugram, Noida from November 5 9 ‘Didn’t want to do anything else’: Why Louise Kennedy studied creative writing and became an author 10 Mukul Kesavan: Growing up in Lutyens’ Delhi – an urban history in anecdotes Author Jaroslavas Melnikas. | Sahitya Akademi Lithuanian writer Jaroslavas Melnikas writes from the edge of certainty. His fictional world is one where reality constantly slips into another, where ordinary lives suddenly confront metaphysical doubt, and where human beings stand suspended between the visible and the invisible. I was drawn to this unsettling world long before I began translating The Last Day into Hindi. These stories not only captivated my literary sensibility but also led me toward self-reflection. The paradoxes and predicaments faced by the characters in this collection were deeply rooted in human consciousness. Melnikas’ characters inhabit unstable realities where everyday life suddenly fractures, exposing loneliness, moral ambiguity, and the fragility of certainty. There was something profoundly familiar in his exploration of existence, freedom, memory, and identity, as though his stories were speaking to anxieties already embedded within me. Lithuanian, one of the oldest surviving European languages, remains relatively unfamiliar in the Indian literary sphere. Melnikas himself occupies a compelling cultural position. Born in western Ukraine and living in Lithuania for the past three decades, he writes in both Ukrainian and Lithuanian, though in recent years Lithuanian has become his primary literary language. His oeuvre, comprising nearly 15 books, is distinguished by a striking fusion of dystopian imagination and surrealism. His writings have been translated into several major European languages, and The Last Day was awarded the BBC Book of the Year European Prize. This collection has eight stories, each of which deepens the sense of human crisis. These are intellectually stimulating and in one sense appear remarkably similar to one another, as though one were reading a single long story that entwines varied human emotions and compels one to think more deeply about the purpose of life. Melnikas is a philosopher at heart; he invariably creates a beautiful interplay between the “real” and the “philosophical”. All the stories in this collection bring out the irony of human life and a deep awareness of existential crisis. Human beings living in deceptively simple circumstances suddenly find themselves in situations that begin to alter the meaning and direction of their lives. External reality starts to seem meaningless, while an unseen reality slowly makes itself felt, one that is as true as the world we can touch and name. We are often caught in the struggle of making constant choices, yet the individuals in these stories discover just how helpless they truly are. Among the stories in the collection, “The Last Day” struck me as the emotional and intellectual centre of Melnikas’s universe. The last day here literally means to possess the knowledge of the exact date of one’s death. What initially appears to be speculative fiction gradually transforms into a profound meditation on how human beings live under the shadow of mortality. The terror in the story does not arise merely from death but from its certainty; the unbearable burden of knowing. The story is about a family – a mother, father and two children who find out about their dates of demise. It is the last day of their young son’s life and they don’t know how to commemorate it. In the end, the family simply sits together and watches a television series. This strange coexistence of routine and catastrophe gives the story its haunting power. The final twist in the story emerges when the clock ticks towards the appointed hour, midnight passes, and the boy does not die. The Book of Fates , it transpires, has stopped working. The father, who had believed he had many more years ahead of him, now understands that he could die tomorrow. Suddenly certainty collapses again, and uncertainty returns almost as a grace. Melnikas suggests that this uncertainty should not alter how one chooses to live. In the end, the family decides to go to the beach not thinking about the future anymore. Translating this movement from fear to release, I found myself returning repeatedly to the reflections on impermanence and illusion in Indian philosophy, particularly the “Nasadiya Sukta” in the Rigveda . What began as an attempt to render Melnikas into another linguistic and cultural register gradually became an inward journey, an excavation of meanings that felt strangely familiar, as though they had long resided in the deeper substratum of my own consciousness. The “Nasadiya Sukta” begins with a striking paradox: there was neither existence nor non-existence, neither death nor immortality, neither sky nor space as we understand them today. The hymn does not offer definitive answers about creation; rather, it culminates in radical doubt – “Who truly knows?” Melnikas’ fictional universe moves through a similar territory. He repeatedly dismantles the structures through which human beings seek stability of time, identity, morality, relationships and even language itself. His characters find themselves caught between realities, unable to determine where the visible world ends and another begins. Reality in these stories is never fixed; it remains unstable, porous, and constantly shifting. In “The Grand Piano Room,” for instance, the protagonist withdraws from the harsh circumstances in which his family struggles to survive and moves inward toward another world, where he seeks the grand piano room. This movement toward an alternate space appears to hold greater meaning than mere existence. The real world comes to seem inhuman and brutal, while the imagined world appears cultured, refined, and deeply desirable. Melnikas is less concerned with constructing dystopian futures than with interrogating the very mechanisms by which reality is perceived and affirmed as truth. Melnikas repeatedly places ordinary individuals in situations where even moral certainty begins to crumble. A man who kills an intruder to save his family soon discovers that legality cannot absolve him of the burden of guilt. He dwells upon the whole situation, probing the psychology of the criminal and the philosophy of criminality alike. One character is a criminal; the other becomes, by accident, a de facto criminal. The author builds the story, “Would You Forgive Me?” with extraordinary skill. The wife is too frightened to sleep beside a man who has just killed someone; he is himself overwhelmed by his action when he encounters the grieving mother and children of the dead man. The incident changes his life, his emotions and his relationships forever. At the end of the story, he goes to the grave of the dead man seeking forgiveness: “I put an end to your journey in this world, my friend. Would you forgive me perhaps?” An ethical negotiation with uncertainty Elsewhere, in other stories as well, people are compelled to make impossible choices between alternatives that are equally unbearable, exposing the illusion of free will itself. His stories resist simplistic divisions between innocence and culpability, victim and perpetrator, sanity and madness. While translating these moments, I often felt that the language itself resisted closure. The emotional terrain of the stories demanded that ambiguity remain intact. Translation here was not merely an act of linguistic transference but an ethical negotiation with uncertainty. I gradually realised that Melnikas’ narratives derive their force precisely from their refusal to resolve human contradictions. His characters continue to inhabit moral tension long after the narrative ends, and the reader remains equally unsettled. Equally striking is the loneliness that pervades his fictional world. His characters move through routines that gradually drain existence of meaning. Relationships become fragile, communication incomplete and intimacy strangely displaced. Human beings long for connection but remain trapped within invisible structures of alienation. Sometimes this loneliness pushes them toward obsessive attachments; sometimes toward imagined realities; sometimes toward silence itself. One of the most haunting aspects of Melnikas’s writing is the way routine itself becomes a form of violence. Everyday life appears capable of eroding human consciousness from within. Several characters experience moments of extreme emotional intensity only to find themselves pulled back into the deadening rhythms of ordinary existence. Melnikas seems deeply aware of the modern condition in which people continue functioning socially while internally experiencing profound exhaustion. At the same time, his stories also interrogate the instability of identity itself. Individuals dissolve into roles, names become fluid, relationships lose fixed definitions, and even authorship becomes uncertain. In one striking instance during the translation process, a character appeared under two different names in the same story, which is a fairly long one running into 50 pages. The man is addressed both as “Serioza” and “Serge.” Initially, this seemed like a confusion in translation, but when I discussed it with Melnikas, he explained that the variation was intentional. “Serge,” he suggested, carried a more romantic and Frenchified resonance. What appeared at first as inconsistency revealed itself as part of his larger resistance to fixed identities and rigid definitions. Another moment that set me thinking was a dialogue in the same story – “Foxie. Don't you remember me? My dear sister . I… His voice trembled.” Here, “my dear sister” is actually the beloved. The usage initially created considerable confusion during translation; however, the author clarified that he wanted to evoke love as an emotion unconfined by conventional relational boundaries. Such moments revealed how fundamentally Melnikas disregards the tyranny of specifics. His writing constantly dissolves categories that human beings normally depend upon for emotional and social stability. A jugalbandi As a translator, I found myself increasingly conscious that the task was not simply to reproduce meaning but to preserve this fluidity of experience. Translation, for me, has always resembled a jugalbandi – a musical dialogue between two artists who respond to, challenge and enrich one another through improvisation. The translator does not mechanically imitate the original; rather, both voices enter into a dynamic relationship that generates something new while retaining fidelity to the spirit of the source. This understanding became particularly important because my translation emerged through mediation. I approached Melnikas through the English translation by Marija Marcinkute, while remaining aware of the inevitable transformations produced by linguistic transition. Initially, I worried that English had somewhat homogenised the fluid movement of tenses present in the original. On the other hand, Hindi offered a surprising flexibility that enabled me to recover some of this shifting temporal texture. Here, the guidance of the Lithuanian Ambassador to India, Diana Mickeviciene, who knows Lithuanian, Hindi and English, proved invaluable. The author too was available for discussions whenever ambiguities arose. A Polish friend and translator, Maria Puri, also contributed insights that enriched my understanding of the cultural and geopolitical nuances surrounding the text. Gradually, the translation evolved into a collaborative process rather than a solitary undertaking. Translator Rekha Sethi. What fascinated me throughout this journey was the discovery that literature continuously transcends national and linguistic boundaries. Initially, I had imagined that the distance between Lithuania and India – culturally, historically and linguistically – might be difficult to bridge. Yet the deeper I entered Melnikas’ world, the more I realised how profoundly shared human anxieties are. His stories did not feel foreign. The loneliness, uncertainty, fear, moral confusion and yearning inhabiting his characters belonged equally to us. Perhaps this is why the act of translation gradually became inseparable from self-reflection. Translating these stories was not merely a literary exercise but an inward movement toward questions that remain unresolved within all human existence. The spaces between words became as important as the words themselves. Silence carried meaning equal to language. One learns, as a translator, to inhabit these silences patiently. The jugalbandi I had imagined at the outset ultimately became a conversation between two philosophical traditions, two literary sensibilities and two ways of understanding human existence. Melnikas writes from a world shaped by Soviet history, European existentialism and the shadow of historical violence. I approached his work from a literary inheritance deeply marked by ambiguity, transcendence and metaphysical inquiry. Between these two worlds, I found not distance, but a sense of recognition. The real and the imaginary are not opposites in Melnikas’ fiction; they are twins. His stories remind us that reality itself may be fragile, provisional and incomplete. They compel us to confront the unresolved question at the centre of human existence: who are we, and how shall we live? In translating Jaroslavas Melnikas, I found myself unexpectedly translating my own anxieties, inheritances and intuitions. What began as an act of literary service gradually revealed itself as something far more intimate, a reckoning with the self. Rekha Sethi is an academic, scholar, translator and editor. Her main area of work is post-independence Hindi poetry and fiction, gender studies and media studies.
